Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that despite Apple's claims to review submissions, blatant rating manipulation on the App Store has gone undetected.

He says he wasn't intentionally searching for scam apps on the App Store, but frequently stumbles upon them by accident, and shared a recent example……

The App Store is a "safe and trusted place"

Apple takes a hardline stance against any antitrust measures involving third-party App Stores or iPhone sideloading, often only relenting when legally compelled. Even so, Apple continues to defend itself.

The company claims this isn't about money, but about protecting iPhone users from malware. For example, Apple said last year that it had blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, many developers question the claim that the App Store is a safe place, pointing to multiple scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers who claimed their Bitcoin was entirely stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store rating manipulation

App Store rating manipulation is a long-standing problem, with some companies even renting "iPhone farms" in mainland China to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for his StopTheMadness Safari extension) noted that he considers this latest case of App Store review manipulation to be "massive and obvious." The app in question is TabControl Extension.

He says that when he stumbled upon this app, it was ranked 12th on the US Mac App Store paid Safari extensions chart, and the screenshots shown were clearly AI-generated fake images.

Another thing worth noting is that the fake screenshot claimed the app had a rating of "4.9 out of 5," misleading people into thinking these were App Store user reviews……Using App Store screenshots for false claims is a common scam tactic, which I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself but also the App Store listing data and metadata, including screenshots. The claims in scam app screenshots are often absurd to the extreme, but Apple approves them anyway……Apple claims the App Store can protect users from dishonest developers. If App Store review can't even detect this kind of issue, then what's the point of review? In fact, App Store review doesn't need to be as thorough as mine. A screenshot claiming "4.9 out of 5" is itself a red flag. Apple has records of all ratings and reviews for every country, so they fully know this is false advertising. I don't even need to download this damn app to know the developer is trying to scam users.

As he says, if a developer is willing to use deceptive tactics to promote their app from the start, you certainly wouldn't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, completely eliminating all App Store scams is impossible, but fake reviews are extremely common, and cases like this one should be obvious to Apple. What's puzzling is how this extension managed to pass review in the first place.

Apple should at least establish a mechanism to automatically conduct stricter reviews on any app that climbs the charts, checking both the app itself and the claims it makes.
